titulo: Pretérito perfecto: saying what you did today: Irregular participles

aula.titulo: Pretérito perfecto: saying what you did today
aula.objetivo: Form the pretérito perfecto with haber + past participle (regular and irregular), use it with hoy, esta mañana, esta semana, ya, todavía no, alguna vez and nunca, and see where it overlaps with — and differs from — the English present perfect.

blocos.titulo: The participles that break the rule
blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: a handful of very common verbs have an irregular participle. There aren't many, and you already know most of them from their infinitive. STEP 2: learn these first: hacer → hecho, decir → dicho, ver → visto, poner → puesto, escribir → escrito, abrir → abierto, volver → vuelto, romper → roto. STEP 3: compound verbs follow their base verb: «deshacer» → deshecho; «describir» → descrito; «devolver» → devuelto. STEP 4: verbs that are irregular in the present often have a perfectly regular participle: ir → ido, ser → sido, estar → estado, tener → tenido, dar → dado, saber → sabido, querer → querido, poder → podido, salir → salido, venir → venido. STEP 5: -er and -ir verbs whose stem ends in a vowel carry an accent on the «í» of the participle: leer → leído, creer → creído, oír → oído, traer → traído, caer → caído. STEP 6: an irregular participle is used exactly the same way: «Hoy he hecho la compra» (today I did the shopping), «Hemos visto una película» (we've watched a movie), «Han escrito un correo» (they've written an email). STEP 7: to practice, answer the question «¿Qué has hecho hoy?» always with «he + participle». STEP 8: in negative sentences with «todavía no», the participle stays exactly the same: «Todavía no he visto la película».
blocos.comparacao: English irregular past participles (seen, done, written, opened) are just as unpredictable as Spanish ones, so the habit of simply memorizing the irregular list transfers directly. The trap here is specific to Spanish: inventing a regular-looking form by false analogy with the infinitive — something like «he hacido» or «he escribido» — which isn't a mistake English speakers would make the same way, since English doesn't build its irregular participles off a predictable suffix pattern to begin with.

erros.motivo: The participle of «leer» carries an accent on the «í».

blocos.enunciado: Say what you've done today, this week, and this month, using six verbs with an irregular participle: «He hecho… He visto… He escrito… He puesto… He abierto… He dicho…»
Conjugate «haber» from memory. Say three sentences with regular participles: one in -ado, one in -ido, and one with a reflexive verb.
